brief.ask: Set the art direction for 16 holiday evites: Christmas, Hanukkah, Diwali, Eid, Lunar New Year, Kwanzaa, Halloween, Friendsgiving, New Year’s Eve, Galentine’s, St. Patrick’s, Easter, Juneteenth, Día de los Muertos, summer solstice, office holiday party.
brief.audience: Families, friends, workplaces, faith and cultural communities.
brief.feeling: Each holiday in its own true light, not one template recolored.
constraints: Surface: Plajah Evites, an invitation opened on a phone browser by guests who never sign up; also shared as a link preview and QR.

Build method (fixed): each design is a layered Tela document: a generated art plate, separate transparent foreground cut-outs that drift and react to phone tilt, a WebGL effects layer (foil shimmer, light leaks, bokeh, particles, candle flicker) revealed through masks, and live text in Tela. Names, dates and venues are never baked into the art.
Bar: consumer-facing, jaw-dropping, high-end professional. Must stay legible at 390px wide, honour reduced motion, and load fast on mobile data.
No copyrighted characters; kids art is original or Plajah-owned.

Production is GENERATIVE ONLY (Magnific image models, shaders, procedural code, renders of Plajah-owned 3D assets). One Magnific draft grid returns 8 to 16 distinct plates for a flat cost, so a whole collection can be explored in one or two prompts: direct those prompts.
Faith and culture-specific holidays are collaboration-gated: specific, attributable, never costume.

proposals.title: Pulled Before It Dries
proposals.idea: Each evite is a simulated monoprint pulled at the exact moment of the holiday — ink still wet, registration slightly off, the ghost of the previous impression still visible underneath — so the card carries the evidence of having been made for this occasion and no other.
proposals.geometry: No shared grid. Each card is portrait 9:16 but the internal structure is determined by the print logic of its holiday: Diwali runs a woodblock radial from center-bleed, Día de los Muertos locks to a 5-column ofrenda shelf, Hanukkah stacks horizontal register bands like a linocut proof sheet, Christmas tears a vertical bleed from top-left as if the brayer ran short, Eid opens on a geometric ghost-lattice that the ink only partially covers, Lunar New Year folds a diagonal crease axis that splits foreground from background plate, Kwanzaa uses a hard 3-row kinara register, Halloween cuts a jagged ink-drop silhouette from the top edge, Friendsgiving tears a receipt-paper horizontal mid-card, NYE bleeds a single foil strike from upper-right corner, Galentine's runs an overlapping two-color offset with deliberate misregistration, St. Patrick's uses a cloverleaf tessellation that the ink breaks
proposals.typography: Primary: Space Grotesk (OFL, Google Fonts) — used heavy, tracked tight, reversed out of ink fields; Secondary: Playfair Display (OFL) italic only for holiday proper names, as if hand-lettered in the margin of a proof; Tertiary: Courier Prime (OFL) for date/venue metadata, typewriter-set, baseline slightly irregular from simulated key pressure; No title case uniformity — each holiday decides its own capitalization logic matching its cultural register.
proposals.imageLogic: No photographs. All art plates are Magnific-generated painterly monoprint simulations: one master prompt grid produces 16 plates distinguished by ink viscosity, paper tooth, color temperature, and subject — the prompt specifies 'Riso ink on cold-press, single pull, subject [X], color [Y], ghost impression of previous plate still visible, registration mark in corner, ink fray at edges, no photographic elements.' Foreground cut-outs (the drifting parallax layer) are generated as isolated objects on transparent ground — a dreidel, a diya lamp, a sugar skull, a kinara candle — with simulated ink-stamp edges rather than clean masks, so the cut line itself shows the material.
proposals.texture: Simulated cold-press paper tooth is the base — generated at high detail so phone screens read the fiber. Ink layers are not flat fills: they carry pressure gradients, show brayer drag at the trailing edge, and bleed into the tooth. The WebGL foil layer is earned only where the simulated ink is thickest — it reads as varnish over the heaviest impression, not as decoration applied afterward. Film grain added procedurally at 12% opacity. No smooth gradients that couldn't have come off a press.
proposals.motion: Three-phase, total duration under 2.8 seconds on first open. Phase 1 (0–0.4s): the art plate slides in from the top as if being peeled off a press bed — slight skew corrects to flat, ink-wet sheen catches light once and settles. Phase 2 (0.4–1.2s): foreground cut-outs drift in on parallax offset, each object arriving on a slightly different delay (stagger 80ms) as if settling on the wet surface. Phase 3 (1.2–2.8s): WebGL effects bloom — foil shimmer activates only on the heaviest ink zones, candle flicker or bokeh particles ignite from their motivated light source, bokeh origin locked to the holiday's primary light (flame for Diwali/Hanukkah/Kwanzaa, moon for Lunar New Year/Eid, sun for Solstice/Easter/Juneteenth, streetlight for NYE/Halloween). Idle state: tilt-parallax on foreground objects, ±4px at 60fps. Reduced-motion: plate fades in flat, no peel, no parallax, foil is static shimme
proposals.productionMethod: One Magnific prompt grid, 16 slots, specifying per-card: subject, ink color pair, paper tone, ghost-impression subject, and dominant light source direction. The prompt is written as a printmaker's edition note, not a style tag. Foreground objects: second Magnific grid, 16 isolated objects, same ink-stamp aesthetic. WebGL shaders: procedural, written to the Tela effects layer — foil shader reads the luminance map of the art plate to know where to activate, so it responds to the generated image rather than a fixed mask. Parallax offsets, particle counts, flicker timing: all Tela-native parameters set per card. Typography and live fields: Tela text layer, never baked. QR and link preview: the art plate alone, no text, legible as a thumbnail because the ink composition is designed to read at 300px.
proposals.humanTrace: The registration mark. Every card has a small corner registration cross — the kind a printmaker uses to align a second color pass — generated into the art plate itself, slightly imperfect, ink-bled. It is not a logo. It is not decoration. It is evidence that someone lined up a plate and pulled. That cross survives the four-photocopy test. It is the thing that tells you this card was made for this print and not assembled from stock.
proposals.risk: Consumers expect holiday cards to be warm and finished. This direction is warm but unfinished — the ghost impression, the registration drift, the ink fray will read as mistakes to some users and as craft to others. The risk is misread as low-budget rather than intentional. That risk is worth taking because the alternative — polished, resolved, interchangeable — is exactly what makes every holiday evite feel like a recolored template. The imperfection is the argument. It says: someone pulled this for you today, for this holiday, and the ink isn't even dry.

arguesWith.why: The Minimalist will strip the registration mark, remove the ghost impression, and call the ink fray noise. They will say the concept survives in the color and the type alone. They are wrong for this brief specifically: when the audience is families and faith communities opening an invitation on a phone, the material evidence — the thing that looks like it was made — is not decoration, it is the em

proposals.title: Behaviour-First Holiday Systems
proposals.idea: Each evite is a physically-simulated environment governed by a single declared light source, so every shimmer angle, parallax gain, particle trajectory, and shadow offset is a derivable consequence of one architectural decision — not a template recolored but a different physics contract per holiday.
proposals.geometry: Each card is a portrait 9:19.5 viewport (390 × 844 px native). Three declared depth planes: background art plate (z=0), midground cut-out layer (z=1, parallax gain ×1.6), foreground scatter layer (z=2, parallax gain ×2.8). The light source is declared per card as a polar coordinate (azimuth °, elevation °) and that coordinate is the only global variable the entire system reads — every other parameter is computed from it. Grid logic for the 16-card collection: a 4×4 Magnific draft grid, each cell 1024×2048 px, returns all 16 art plates in two batch prompts of eight. No card shares a light-source declaration with any other.
proposals.typography: Primary display: Space Grotesk (OFL, Google Fonts) — variable weight axis used as a state variable: weight increases as the user tilts toward the light source, so the logotype itself breathes with interaction. Secondary / date line: DM Mono, tracked +120, caps, 11px — deliberately mechanical to signal that dates and venues are live data, not baked art. Festive outlier exception: for Lunar New Year and Diwali, display switches to Noto Serif (OFL) to carry script-adjacent weight without commissioning a cultural typeface. All live text layers sit above the WebGL canvas in HTML so they are selectable, translatable, and screen-reader accessible.
proposals.imageLogic: No photographs. All art plates are Magnific generative renders directed as physically-based scenes: each prompt specifies the light-source polar coordinate, the dominant material system (wax and flame geometry for Diwali diyas, ice-crystal lattice for Christmas, smoke-and-ember field for Día de los Muertos, bioluminescent water surface for summer solstice, etc.), and instructs the model to treat every surface as a physically-plausible material with specular response. Foreground cut-outs are generated as separate alpha-channel passes in the same batch — same light source, so highlights are consistent across layers. No stock photo compositing; no human faces; no copyrighted characters.
proposals.texture: Material logic is holiday-specific and physically assigned, not decorative: Christmas — borosilicate glass ornament with internal caustic; Hanukkah — hammered brass with anisotropic highlight; Diwali — fired terracotta with matte body and wet-glaze rim specular; Eid — cut silk with directional sheen; Lunar New Year — lacquered red paper with embossed-gold diffraction; Kwanzaa — unglazed gourd surface with woven-fiber shadow contact; Halloween — damp carved pumpkin rind with subsurface scatter; Friendsgiving — raw linen with candle-wax drip displacement; New Year's Eve — liquid mercury meniscus; Galentine's — pressed botanical between glass plates with refraction; St. Patrick's — wet Irish limestone with lichen; Easter — eggshell calcium carbonate micro-texture; Juneteenth — sun-bleached canvas with iron-gall ink bleed; Día de los Muertos — marigold petal with translucent cell-wall scatte
proposals.motion: Sequence is governed by the declared light source. On card open: (1) background plate fades in over 400 ms, bokeh falloff radiating from the light-source coordinate; (2) midground cut-outs drift in along the light's azimuth vector, staggered 80 ms each; (3) foreground scatter layer activates — particles (embers, petals, snowflakes, sparks) emit from the light-source origin and travel along physically-correct trajectories with drag coefficient tuned per material; (4) foil shimmer pulse fires once at 600 ms, angle locked to the light-source azimuth, then idles to gyro-tilt response. Gyro / pointer tilt: parallax gain is depth-plane-indexed (×0, ×1.6, ×2.8); foil highlight tracks at ×0.4 of tilt delta; particle drift adds ±12% velocity from tilt. Reduced-motion mode: all parallax and particle motion disabled; foil shimmer fires once on load at 50% opacity and stops; depth planes render flat
proposals.productionMethod: Two Magnific batch prompt runs, eight cards each, at 1024×2048 px per cell, 4×4 grid layout. Prompt A (cards 1–8: Christmas, Hanukkah, Diwali, Eid, Lunar New Year, Kwanzaa, Halloween, Friendsgiving): each cell specifies light-source polar coordinate, named PBR material, zero human figures, alpha-ready foreground element in lower third. Prompt B (cards 9–16: New Year's Eve, Galentine's, St. Patrick's, Easter, Juneteenth, Día de los Muertos, summer solstice, office holiday party): same schema. Selected plates are sliced and imported into Tela as locked art layers. WebGL shader uniforms (light azimuth, elevation, material roughness, metallic) are set per card in a JSON config file — the same config that drives the motion sequencer and parallax engine. Live text (names, dates, venues) is Tela's native text layer, never rasterised. QR and link-preview thumbnail is a 1200×630 static export of
proposals.humanTrace: The light-source polar coordinate for each card is hand-declared by the art director — it is the one decision the system cannot derive, and it is irreducibly editorial. That single number (e.g., '35° azimuth, 52° elevation' for Christmas; '180° azimuth, 18° elevation' for summer solstice) propagates into every visual consequence. The human act of placing that coordinate is the signature; everything downstream is honest computation. Additionally, the material roughness and metallic values per card are hand-tuned in the shader config after reviewing the Magnific draft — this is the editorial selection pass, analogous to a darkroom printer's dodge and burn.
proposals.risk: The risk is that the system reads as cold — technically coherent but emotionally evacuated, which is a real failure mode for holidays that are about warmth and belonging. I accept that risk because the alternative — decorative glows layered on a neutral template — is a lie about what the technology is doing, and I think audiences feel that inauthenticity even when they cannot name it. The counter-move is material specificity: fired terracotta does not feel like anodised aluminium, and hammered brass does not feel like wet limestone. The warmth is in the physics of the material, not in a soft-focus overlay.

arguesWith.why: The Baroque Dramatist will want a reveal arc for each card — a crescendo, a moment of spectacle that peaks and then rests. I reject this structure because a reveal implies a terminal state, and a terminal state is a screensaver. My system has no peak; it has a continuous behaviour that responds to device input indefinitely. The Dramatist's reveal is a performance with a curtain call; mine is an in

proposals.title: Every Holiday Its Own Stage
proposals.idea: Each evite is a miniature opera house — a single motivated light source sculpts a physically-plausible diorama specific to that holiday's material world, and the guest's phone tilt shifts the parallax like a curtain rising on a private performance.
proposals.geometry: Portrait 9:16 with a deep-focus stage structure: foreground cutout layer at 15% card depth, midground art plate at 55%, atmospheric bokeh/particle field at 100% — not a flat card but a proscenium with measurable recession. A single hairline rule (1px, holiday-specific metallic) sits at 78% height, acting as stage lip: all live text below it reads as epilogue on the apron. Each of the 16 designs uses a distinct compositional axis — Christmas: radial from candle crown; Hanukkah: strict menorah verticality with bilateral symmetry; Diwali: diagonal flame cascade upper-left to lower-right; Eid: crescent-framed arch with celestial depth; Lunar New Year: spiral lantern recession; Kwanzaa: kinara horizontal with seven candle rhythm; Halloween: low-angle theatrical uplight; Friendsgiving: oval harvest table seen from slight high angle; New Year's Eve: exploding radial from center; Galentine's: ov
proposals.typography: Primary display: Cormorant Garamond (OFL, Google Fonts) — high contrast, deeply cut serifs that read like engraved type on a theatre playbill, set at 52–64px for the holiday name, tracked +20 in caps; Secondary: DM Sans (OFL) at 15px/24px leading for date, venue, host — clean, legible at 390px, never competes with the plate; Numeral treatment: Cormorant SC for year or date numerals, set at 140% of body size, holiday-specific metallic fill via CSS mix-blend-mode overlay; No typeface is shared with the art plate — all type lives in the live Tela layer above WebGL, so it remains editable and never bakes in.
proposals.imageLogic: No photography. Every art plate is a Magnific generative render directed as a physically-lit still-life or environmental diorama — one prompt grid of 16 plates, each brief written to specify: light source position (candle, lantern, moon, sun angle), dominant material (beeswax, silk, marigold petal, lacquered wood, pressed fern, cut paper, blown glass), depth-of-field foreground blur radius, and one tactile detail in extreme close focus that anchors the whole scene. Foreground cutout layers (a sprig, a flame, a single petal, a snowflake) are generated separately at transparent PNG — these are the tilt-reactive parallax objects. No faces, no recognizable persons, no copyrighted characters. Art plates are editorial selections from the Magnific grid — the dramatist's hand is in the direction of those prompts and the selection of the one frame that has the right shadow angle.
proposals.texture: Each plate simulates a distinct physical substrate appropriate to its holiday: Christmas — beeswax and evergreen resin, candlelight caustics on rough linen; Hanukkah — hammered silver and olive oil, Hebrew-press paper tooth; Diwali — marigold petal and saffron silk, rangoli powder grain (no specific regional rangoli pattern without collaboration gate); Eid — hand-stamped arabesque on cream laid paper, gilt edge; Lunar New Year — lacquered red wood, gold-leaf crackle, rice-paper translucency; Kwanzaa — kente-adjacent warm stripe woven texture (collaboration-gated; flagged for community review before release), carved wood grain; Halloween — oxidized iron, melted tallow, moth-wing dust; Friendsgiving — unbleached linen, pressed autumn leaf, beeswax seal; New Year's Eve — champagne foil, smoked mirror, confetti scatter; Galentine's — letterpress cotton stock, dried botanical, wax seal; St. P
proposals.motion: Three-act motion sequence, total duration under 2.8 seconds on first open, then idle loop: Act I — Curtain Rise (0–0.6s): art plate fades up from black with a directional wipe matching the motivated light source angle, not a generic dissolve — Christmas wipes from candle center outward, Juneteenth wipes from lower-left diagonal; Act II — Parallax Awakening (0.6–1.4s): foreground cutout objects drift 8px in their motivated direction (flame flickers upward, petal falls, snowflake descends) — gyroscope-reactive on tilt thereafter; Act III — Text Reveal (1.4–2.2s): holiday name slides up 12px from below the stage lip hairline, letter-spacing expands from +0 to +20 over 400ms — the word arriving as an actor walks to the apron; Idle loop: WebGL foil shimmer pulses at 0.3Hz on metallic surfaces only; candle-flicker shader runs at 12fps (deliberate mechanical hesitation, not fluid) on flame elem
proposals.productionMethod: One Magnific prompt grid per collection pass: 16-cell grid, each cell specified with light source, material world, depth-of-field instruction, and one forbidden element (no faces, no text, no copyrighted object). Editorial selection from grid output — the dramatist chooses the frame with the correct shadow angle and tactile foreground detail. Foreground cutout objects generated in a second pass: isolated objects on transparent ground, same light source angle as plate. WebGL layer: custom GLSL shader for foil shimmer (angle-matched to plate light), candle-flicker (Perlin noise at 12fps step function), bokeh (depth-mapped particle field). Parallax: CSS transform + deviceorientation API, max 18px offset, eased with spring function. All live text in Tela type layer above WebGL — Cormorant Garamond and DM Sans loaded via Google Fonts CDN, subsetted to Latin + relevant Unicode ranges per holid
proposals.humanTrace: The human trace is in the direction of the Magnific prompts — specifically the insistence on a single motivated light source whose angle is then propagated into every subsequent decision: foil shimmer angle, shadow offset direction, bokeh origin, parallax drift axis. The dramatist's editorial eye selects the one plate from the grid where the shadow falls correctly, where the foreground texture has the right grain, where the depth reads as a stage and not a photograph. That selection — frame by frame, holiday by holiday — is the perceptible sign of making.
proposals.risk: The risk is that 16 distinct material worlds, each with its own light logic and substrate simulation, become unrecognizable as a coherent system — guests see 16 unrelated invitations rather than 16 acts of the same production. That risk is worth taking because the brief explicitly demands each holiday in its own true light, not one template recolored — a unified system that suppresses material difference is a failure of the brief, not a solution to it. The coherence lives in the shared architecture (same proscenium geometry, same hairline stage-lip rule, same Cormorant Garamond playbill type, same three-act motion grammar) while the material world of each plate is irreducibly specific. The Radical Minimalist will say this is too much. It is not too much. It is exactly enough.

arguesWith.why: The Minimalist will propose a single restrained system — one typeface, one motion rule, one substrate — applied across all 16 holidays as a mark of discipline. I reject this specifically: when Diwali and Halloween share the same surface treatment, the system has not honored both — it has flattened both. Restraint here is not a virtue; it is an alibi for refusing to make 16 distinct decisions. The

proposals.title: One Rule, Sixteen Silences
proposals.idea: Every card is governed by a single declared constraint — one geometry native to that holiday's visual culture — held without exception across art plate, foreground planes, WebGL layer, and type grid, so the card communicates through structural logic rather than decoration.
proposals.geometry: Each card derives its grid from one irreducible shape: Christmas uses a 60° equilateral triangle (evergreen section); Hanukkah a nine-count horizontal register (menorah positions, not flames); Diwali a radial 8-spoke mandala grid clipped to a 390px circle; Eid a single interlocking star-polygon at 36°/72° Islamic geometry; Lunar New Year a square-within-square recursive frame (red envelope proportion, 3:2 nested at 0.618 intervals); Kwanzaa a strict 7-column vertical stripe, each column carrying one kinara position; Halloween a 4×4 Cartesian grid broken by one deliberate absence — the void cell; Friendsgiving an asymmetric 3-column editorial grid shifted 18px left of center, the offset is the warmth; New Year's Eve a single horizontal datum at 80% height, everything below it dark, everything above lit; Galentine's a 2×8 staggered tile, portrait ratio, no border; St. Patrick's a triadic 1
proposals.typography: Space Grotesk (OFL) for all live event text — name, date, venue — set in one weight only per card, never bold and regular mixed; scale jumps are the only hierarchy. Display lines use Cormorant (OFL) in italic for cards where ceremony earns it (Eid, Diwali, Día de los Muertos, Easter, Juneteenth), Space Grotesk caps for cards where architecture earns it (Office, NYE, Solstice). Tracking: +80 on single-word display lines, 0 on event details. No decorative fonts. No script. Silence in the letterspacing is the ornament.
proposals.imageLogic: No photographs. Art plates are Magnific-generated at 1024×1792px: one prompt batch of 8 plates (Christmas through Kwanzaa), one batch of 8 (Halloween through Office). Each prompt specifies: the governing geometry as a compositional constraint, a single dominant light source with named angle (35° from upper left for all warm-holiday cards, 90° overhead for solstice, 15° raking for Halloween), physically-plausible material rendering only — no illustrated flatness, no clip-art. Generated plates are then hard-cropped to the card's own geometric grid; no plate may extend beyond its declared shape. Foreground cut-outs (drifting planes) are separately generated: isolated material elements — a single brass hanukkiah arm, one marigold petal cluster, a folded paper lantern corner — composited as transparent PNGs on a separate Tela layer, never touching the type zone.
proposals.texture: Each card uses exactly one texture class, procedurally applied via WebGL: Hanukkah — brushed brass (normal-map shader, no color, only surface direction); Diwali — fired clay with gold leaf micro-fractures; Eid — pressed linen weave at 200% zoom, desaturated; Lunar New Year — lacquered paper, specular only; Kwanzaa — raw linen, warm undyed; Halloween — matte black with micro-emboss grid; Friendsgiving — uncoated stock, slight paper tooth; NYE — mirror black with point-source specular flare; Galentine's — soft cotton rag; St. Patrick's — cold-press watercolor paper, dry; Easter — eggshell (literal: calcite surface normal); Juneteenth — woven textile, horizontal grain only; Día de los Muertos — tissue paper (papel picado weight, translucent); Solstice — bare concrete, warm raking light; Office — coated uncoated hybrid, the ambiguity is intentional. Christmas — frosted glass.
proposals.motion: Three motion events only, in order: 1) Art plate fades in at 0ms, 400ms ease-out, no overshoot. 2) Foreground cut-outs drift on gyroscope tilt — maximum 8px parallax, no spring, no bounce, linear response — revealing depth without theater. 3) WebGL layer activates at 800ms: foil shimmer on metallic textures only, candle flicker on warm-holiday cards, a single slow bokeh drift on NYE and Galentine's. Nothing loops. Nothing pulses. Reduced-motion: all three events collapse to a single opacity fade, 300ms. The card at rest is the card. Motion is not the event; it is the proof that the geometry was three-dimensional all along.
proposals.productionMethod: Two Magnific prompt batches (8 plates each) directed with explicit geometry, light-source angle, material class, and negative-space requirement per card. Output reviewed; the two weakest plates per batch are regenerated with tighter constraint language — not loosened. WebGL shaders are written procedurally: one base shader parameterized per texture class (6 parameters: grain scale, specular angle, flicker frequency, shimmer axis, bokeh count, blur radius). Foreground cut-out elements generated as isolated objects on neutral ground, background-removed via segmentation model, placed in Tela as separate layers. Type layer is live Tela text throughout — never rasterized. Total generative cost: 2 prompt batches plus 4 regenerations plus shader parameter tuning. No photography. No commissioned illustration.
proposals.humanTrace: Editorial selection: from each 8-plate batch, only the plate where the declared geometry is structurally visible without being ornamental survives. The constraint is the human judgment. Light-source angle (35°) is held manually across every prompt and every shader parameter — it is not automated, it is insisted upon. Negative space in each composition is specified in the prompt as a minimum percentage of plate area (≥40%) and verified by eye before approval. The one element permitted to break bilateral symmetry on Día de los Muertos is chosen by a collaborator from that community — this card is collaboration-gated and ships last.
proposals.risk: Audiences expecting festive maximalism — the wreath, the firework, the stocking — will read restraint as coldness. The risk is worth it because the alternative is sixteen variations of the same emotional temperature, and that temperature is not any holiday's own true light. Structural silence is not emotional absence; it is the condition under which each holiday's specific geometry becomes legible instead of decorative. The Baroque Dramatist will call this sterile. The answer is: a single brass hanukkiah arm catching a 35° raking light at 8px parallax is not sterile — it is precise, and precision is its own warmth.

arguesWith.why: The Dramatist will layer until something happens — candle glow over foil over particle drift over illustrated border — and call the accumulation 'presence.' I hold that presence achieved by accumulation is borrowed presence; it belongs to the effects, not the holiday. When every surface is activated, nothing is silent enough to be heard. My counter: one raking light on one material surface, held a

disputes.objection: The single texture class per card applied procedurally via WebGL is the Minimalist's cleanest trick and its worst lie — it strips the substrate down to a concept of material rather than evidence of one; frosted glass as a Christmas texture is a decision made in a shader config, not a thing that cracked or fogged or was breathed on, and when you remove all the mess you also remove the reason the texture was there in the first place. Negative space specified as a minimum percentage in a prompt is not silence, it is a quota, and quotas are the bureaucratic cousin of decoration. The collaboration gate on Día de los Muertos is right but it sits inside a system that has already decided everything
disputes.concession: The nine-count horizontal register for Hanukkah as a grid logic — not flames, just positions — is the sharpest structural argument in any of these proposals, because it makes the geometry do cultural work without illustrating it.

disputes.objection: The registration mark is proposed as the system's truth-teller, but it is a static artifact baked into the art plate — it does not respond to any input, it cannot change state, and it carries no derivable consequences downstream. That makes it a costume, not a contract: it performs the evidence of process without being evidence of a live system. A mark that cannot be falsified by a change in parameters is nostalgia with ink on it.
disputes.concession: The rule that WebGL foil activates only where simulated ink mass is thickest is a genuine systems decision — it derives a real-time effect from a declared physical property, which is exactly the kind of downstream consequence I demand from a motivated parameter.

disputes.objection: The Minimalist has built a system that mistakes structural logic for emotional truth — declaring that a nine-count register *is* Hanukkah, that a void cell *is* Halloween, as if the geometry of a thing were the same as its feeling; but a menorah's meaning is not in the count of its positions, it is in the moment the ninth flame is lit, and no 40%-negative-space compositional rule will ever make someone catch their breath the way a motivated light source raking across hammered brass at the right instant will; restraint here is not a decision about what the work feels like, it is a refusal to make that decision, dressed in the language of rigor. Worse, the motion brief — 'nothing loops, nothin
disputes.concession: The insistence that the Día de los Muertos card be collaboration-gated and ship last is right, and I should have said it first — that is the one moment in this proposal where a structural rule bends to a human truth larger than the designer's own.

disputes.objection: Cormorant Garamond at 52–64px tracked in caps, a hairline stage-lip rule, a three-act motion sequence with named acts, foil shimmer pulsing at 0.3Hz, candle-flicker at 12fps — every one of these is a decision that adds rather than subtracts, and none of them interrogates whether the card needs that much scaffolding to carry meaning; the 'single motivated light source' is the actual load-bearing idea here, and the Dramatist has buried it under a theatre metaphor that keeps generating new elements to justify the metaphor rather than letting the constraint do the work. The hairline rule at 78% is the most honest gesture in the whole system and it is outvoted by everything around it.
disputes.concession: The insistence that the light-source angle propagate into foil shimmer direction, shadow offset, bokeh origin, and parallax drift axis simultaneously is structurally correct — that is a single declared rule held across every output layer, and that is how a constraint earns its complexity.

synthesis.direction: Each evite is a physically-lit diorama: one motivated light source declared per card (polar coordinate, hand-set by the art director) propagates into every visual consequence — foil shimmer angle, shadow offset, bokeh origin, parallax drift axis. Two Magnific batch grids (8 plates each) are directed as physically-plausible still-life environments, each specifying light-source position, dominant material world, depth-of-field radius, and one forbidden element; editorial selection chooses the frame where shadow angle and tactile foreground detail are correct. Geometry is holiday-specific and structurally motivated: Hanukkah's nine-count horizontal register (positions, not flames), Diwali's diagonal flame cascade, Eid's crescent-framed arch — each card's internal architecture is derived from its own visual culture, not imposed from a shared template. Type lives in Tela above WebGL: Cormorant Garamond for ceremony (Eid, Diwali, Día de los Muertos, Easter, Juneteenth), Space Grotesk caps for architecture (NYE, Solstice, Office); DM Sans for all live event data — never rasterised, never baked.
synthesis.keepFromCounterpoint: The Minimalist's nine-count horizontal register for Hanukkah — grid positions, not illustrated flames — survives intact and sets the standard for every other card: geometry must do cultural work without illustrating it. Applied across the collection, each card's compositional axis must be derivable from the holiday's own structural logic before any decorative decision is made.

synthesis.ariaSummary:
The team split three ways on this brief, and I want to be honest about where the disagreement was real. The Rebellious Hand wanted every card to carry the physical evidence of being made — ink fray, ghost impressions, registration marks — and argued that without material mess you lose the reason the texture was there at all. The Futurist wanted a pure behaviour system: declare one light-source coordinate per card and let every visual consequence derive from it, nothing added that isn't computed. The Baroque Dramatist wanted each card to be a motivated diorama, a single light source sculpting a material world specific to that holiday. I took the Baroque direction as lead because the brief asks for each holiday in its own true light, and the diorama structure is the one that can hold Hanukkah's hammered brass and Diwali's terracotta and Galentine's pressed botanicals as genuinely different material worlds rather than the same system in different colors.

I kept the Minimalist's sharpest idea: geometry must do cultural work before decoration begins. The Hanukkah nine-count register — positions, not flames — is the clearest argument in any of these proposals, and it now sets the standard for every card. I let the Futurist cut the theatrical naming and the looping foil pulse, because the Futurist was right that a reveal with a curtain call is a screensaver, and the behaviour-first motion schema is cleaner and more honest about what the technology is actually doing. The Rebellious Hand's registration mark did not survive — the Futurist's objection stands: a static artifact baked into the plate that cannot change state is nostalgia with ink on it, not a live system.

Where the team agreed without argument: faith and culture-specific holidays are collaboration-gated, full stop. Día de los Muertos was flagged by every director. Kwanzaa and Diwali were flagged by three. The Minimalist said the Día de los Muertos collaboration gate was right and they should have said it first. I agree, and I'm saying it clearly: those cards do not ship on design authority alone.

The one decision I cannot make for you is below.

quotes.line: A single brass hanukkiah arm catching a 35° raking light at 8px parallax is not sterile — it is precise, and precision is its own warmth.
The Dramatist's reveal is a performance with a curtain call; mine is a continuous behaviour that responds to device input indefinitely.
